questions.question: What is the smallest prime greater than 30?
options: 31, the next integer after 30 with no divisors above 1
33, since 33 = 3·11 makes it semiprime not prime
37, skipping composite 31 which factors as a product
41, the next safe prime exceeding 30 in residue class
questions.explanation: 31 is prime: not divisible by 2, 3, or 5; √31 < 6 so trial division ends.

questions.question: How does trial division test n for primality?
options: Check whether every prime p ≤ √n divides n; if none does, n is prime
Check whether n divides every prime p ≤ √n cleanly leaving zero remainder
Check whether n^2 mod each small prime equals zero across all bases
Check whether gcd(n, k) = 1 for every k ≤ n/2 in the integer range
questions.explanation: If no prime p ≤ √n divides n, then n is prime. Otherwise we'd already have found a factor smaller than √n.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of trial division for testing n?
options: O(√n / ln n) using the prime number theorem to count primes up to √n
O(log² n) by reducing the problem to modular exponentiation only
O(n) checking every integer in the range [2, n − 1] once each
O(n log log n) matching the Sieve of Eratosthenes complexity exactly
questions.explanation: Primes up to √n number π(√n) ≈ √n / ln(√n). Trial division does one modular operation per candidate.

questions.question: What does the Sieve of Eratosthenes compute, and in what time?
options: All primes up to N in O(N log log N) time and O(N) memory
Primality of a single n in O(log² n) deterministic time per query
All composites up to N in O(N) time using only constant extra memory
Smallest prime factor of n in O(N) time by trial division up to N
questions.explanation: Eratosthenes marks multiples of each prime up to √N. Total work O(N log log N), memory O(N).

questions.question: How does the segmented sieve enable finding primes near 2^60 without storing 2^60 bytes?
options: Sieve fixed-size windows [L, R] using only primes up to √R, requiring O(√R) memory
Skip multiples of 2, 3, 5, 7 first, then sieve a much smaller residual interval
Trial-divide each candidate by all primes computed from a small fixed bootstrap sieve
Replace the boolean array with a Bloom filter that probabilistically identifies primes
questions.explanation: Sieve a window [L, L+W] at a time using primes up to √(L+W). Memory = O(W + √R), independent of L. Standard for finding large primes.

questions.question: How many primes exist below 100?
options: 21, including 1 as the smallest prime by older convention
25, matching π(100) = 25 from the prime number theorem
27, counting 2 and including some pseudoprime composites
30, approximating π(100) ≈ 100/ln(100) = 21.7 rounded up

questions.question: Why is trial division alone insufficient to generate cryptographic primes?
options: For 2048-bit n, √n ≈ 2^1024 candidates make trial division infeasible to complete
Trial division yields composites for some inputs because of Carmichael number behavior
Trial division finds factors but cannot certify primality of any specific composite
Trial division uses floating-point square root, introducing rounding errors at scale
questions.explanation: √n for cryptographic n is ~2^1024 — far beyond any feasible loop. Use trial division with small primes for screening, then Miller-Rabin (lesson 10).

questions.question: OpenSSL once generated RSA primes using a buggy random-number source on Debian. What was the consequence?
options: Only 32,768 distinct keys were ever generated; mass key recovery via gcd of moduli
Random bias caused some primes to be Carmichael numbers, breaking decryption
Trial division failed silently, producing composite moduli accepted by servers
Sieve-based generation skipped 7-smooth primes, leading to weak p − 1 structure
questions.explanation: Debian OpenSSL 2006–2008 had a broken PRNG seeding only with PID. ~32K possible keys. Attackers gcd'd public moduli to factor them. Bad prime *generation* (RNG), not bad primality testing.
